title: How much is the sum that climbs to a hundred and falls back?
description: A sum climbs from one up to one hundred and falls back to one. A huge tilted grid of dots stands for it, so the top number gives the total without adding. Every number of the sum is one slanting row of the grid.
teaching_notes: One idea: an up and down sum to a number is that number times itself, however large the number. Watch for students who add the top number to itself instead of multiplying.

source: Figure it Out Q2 (Try This), p.8
video_script.why: The child finds the value of a very long up and down sum by imagining a large tilted grid, using the top number times itself as in the book's solved example.
video_script.substitution: The top number is one hundred instead of seven.
video_script.anchor: a very large square grid of dots, tilted, drawn only in part
video_script.payoff_line: Going up to one hundred and back down adds up to ten thousand
maths_rules: up and down to n gives n x n, so the grid is 100 by 100
check on a small case: 1 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 9 = 3 x 3
video_script.design: The sum is written with dots in the middle. A large grid is drawn only in part, with its first and last slanting rows shown, then the rule is used.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; the long sum 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + 99 + 100 + 99 + ... + 3 + 2 + 1 is written in one line

marks.book: the small title card From your book appears
marks.sum: the long sum is written, with dots hiding the middle numbers
marks.ask: a question mark appears after the sum

beats.colours: numbers going up in blue, numbers coming down in orange
narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about a very long sum.
<bookmark mark='sum'/>It climbs from one up to one hundred, and then falls back down to one.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Adding nearly two hundred numbers one by one would take very long. What is the value of this sum?

beats.on_screen: the long sum stays on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board as the child

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

beats.on_screen: part of a very large tilted square grid of dots: the top rows and the bottom rows are drawn, the middle is left as dots

marks.way: the sum moves to the side
marks.grid: a large tilted grid appears, drawn only in part
marks.rows: each slanting row is matched with one number of the sum

beats.colours: dots in blue, matched rows in gold
narration: <bookmark mark='way'/>We use the same way as the example in your book.
<bookmark mark='grid'/>Picture a huge square grid of dots, tilted, so we only draw a part of it.
<bookmark mark='rows'/>Each slanting row of dots matches one number of the sum.

marks.given: the long sum is written under the word Given

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the sum climbs from one up to one hundred and falls back to one.

beats.on_screen: To find: the value of the whole sum
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the value of this whole sum.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: top number of the sum = 100, so the grid is 100 by 100

marks.top: the largest number, 100, is circled in gold
marks.side: 100 is set as the side of the grid, 100 by 100

narration: <bookmark mark='top'/>Step one, find the top number, because it is the side of the grid. <bookmark mark='side'/>The top number is one hundred, so the grid is one hundred by one hundred.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: up to a number and back down = that number x itself, so here 100 x 100

marks.values: the top number 100 is put into the rule, giving 100 x 100

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Step two, count all the dots of the grid. A sum that goes up to a number and back down is that number times itself.
<bookmark mark='values'/>Here we multiply one hundred by one hundred.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: check the rule on a small case: 1 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 9 and 3 x 3 = 9

marks.check: the small sum and 3 x 3 are written side by side with the same total

narration: <bookmark mark='check'/>Step three, check the rule on a small case. Up to three and back is nine, and three times three is nine too.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>Going up to one hundred and back down adds up to ten thousand. That is the value of the whole sum.
